 / Automakers Frequently Targeted by Scams, What's Wrong with Auto Recalls? 
 China auto market Automakers Frequently Targeted by Scams, What's Wrong with Auto Recalls?
 Edited by Betty From Gasgoo | November 20 , 2026 22:51 BJT f SHARE TWEET in SHARE SHARE Scan for mobile SAIC-GM Brands Buick, Cadillac, Chevrolet Access Main products Precision machining Gasgoo Munich- Over a recent 10-day span, a string of automakers — including Volkswagen China, SAIC-GM, Volvo, Chery, Great Wall, Li Auto, and Xiaomi — issued strikingly similar statements warning consumers about fraudulent recall notices using their names. These fake notices often forge corporate seals, falsely claim defects in steering systems or airbags, and trick owners into applying for "recall compensation." Meanwhile, the State Administration for Market Regulation (SAMR) has reminded the public that all recalls conducted by automakers are completely free of charge.
 The impersonated brands span joint ventures, luxury marques, and EV startups. In a short period, over 20 companies have issued similar warnings.
 Why have recalls become a target for scammers? What fraudsters are really eyeing is the public's heightened attention to the word "recall." From massive recalls involving millions of vehicles to high-profile models getting caught up in them, and down to specific controversies like hidden door handles — these frequent incidents have pushed "recalls" into the spotlight. Behind this wave of discussion lies an industry-wide logic: in pursuit of speed, automakers are compressing R&D cycles and deferring product validation, ultimately shifting defects downstream to the market.
 Recalls: Why a Target? 
 A recall is fundamentally a regulatory procedure between automakers and authorities: filing, announcing, notifying, and repairing. The average owner only enters the picture at the "notification" stage, usually understanding it simply as "the car has a problem, and the manufacturer will fix it."
 This year, however, the term has entered the mainstream consumer lexicon and become a subject of constant debate.
 Image source: Generated by Doubao
 In 2025, China conducted 190 auto recalls covering 6.846 million vehicles, down 18.5% and 39.1% year-on-year, respectively. In the first half of 2026, there were 50 recalls involving about 1.65 million vehicles — the lowest for the period in a decade.
 By the numbers, recall scale has slipped from previous years, yet public discourse has surged. Clearly, other factors are pushing recalls into the public eye.
 First is the sheer scale of single recalls. On August 21, nine automakers filed recalls on the same day over the identical door handle issue, covering over 4.27 million vehicles — the largest batch recall triggered by a single problem in China. Previously, recalls typically involved tens of thousands of vehicles.
 Amplifying the matter were the models involved. The recall covered 20 models, including the Tesla Model Y, Xiaomi SU7, ZEEKR 007, Leapmotor C01, Leapmotor C11, and XPENG G6. Tesla alone accounted for over 2.97 million vehicles — nearly 70% of the total — while Xiaomi had about 390,000, Leapmotor over 370,000, and XPENG 260,000. Brands like Tesla and Xiaomi are already fixtures in the public eye; their names on a recall notice naturally draw outsized attention.
 Hidden door handles have long been a sticking point. Widely adopted for their sleek design and aerodynamic benefits, they pose a risk in collisions: if the vehicle's low-voltage system fails, the exterior handles may not deploy, hindering rescue efforts. While interior emergency mechanical releases don't rely on power, they are often hard to find and use due to their concealed placement and colors that blend into the interior. This recall aims to patch that exact gap — by adding warning labels so the emergency release can be located and pulled even during a power failure.
 What truly elevated recalls from isolated cases to an industry-wide debate was a controversy over the past few months. Since the second half of the year, "rush-job cars" — vehicles built too quickly — has become an unavoidable topic.
 The topic took center stage at the Chengdu Motor Show in August, where SAIC Volkswagen flashed "No Rush-Job Cars" on its presentation screen, fueling the debate. By October 10, four government bodies, including the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT), sought public input on strengthening automotive design and R&D validation. Li Yanwei, an expert committee member at the China Automobile Dealers Association, interpreted the move as a regulatory shift: authorities are moving upstream from "does the product meet standards" to "was the R&D fully validated," linking R&D identification, filing verification, and mass-production consistency. "This is much closer to the actual root causes of auto safety issues than just looking at a final compliance report," he noted.
 Almost simultaneously, several auto executives spoke out. Li Shufu, chairman of Geely Holding Group, warned that "we cannot apply a fast-and-loose philosophy to car manufacturing. Taking shortcuts will lead to endless trouble." He Zhiqi lamented that "it's gone completely mad — these are cars," while Li Fenggang bluntly stated that "consumers have been turned into test drivers."
 Different words, same target: cars are being built too fast, and validation can't keep up. Recalls are no longer isolated incidents but a cross-section of an entire development rhythm under scrutiny.
 On October 22, regulators weighed in. Li Changqing, a second-level inspector at SAMR, told the World Intelligent Connected Vehicles Conference that the industry must "put an end to the short-sighted behavior of sacrificing safety for speed to market," adding that "inadequately validated products must never be allowed on the road in a hurry" and "marketing must not become a fig leaf for safety hazards." Previously, "speed" was a competitive edge; now, regulators have placed it squarely in the category of safety risks.
 By the end of 2025, China had conducted 3,265 cumulative recalls involving 121 million vehicles. Given a fleet of 370 million cars, roughly one in three owners has experienced a recall. For the general public, a growing number of real-world examples prove that recalls are no longer a distant concept.
 As these factors compound, the public perception of "recalls" has shifted. What was once a notice to be verified is now assumed to be real, urgent, and actionable. This shift has undoubtedly lowered the cost of persuasion for scammers. Fraudsters no longer need to work hard to establish credibility; they simply need to insert themselves into an already accepted scenario.
 " Recalls ": The Real Shift Goes Beyond Numbers 
 As smart connected vehicles evolve, the very nature of the "recall" is changing.
 Historically, recalls happened at the very end of the pipeline: design, validation, production, sales — and only after vehicles hit the road and batch issues surfaced did a recall occur. Today, because many software features can be refined via over-the-air (OTA) updates, automakers have effectively deferred the "validation" stage. Tests and fixes once completed before launch are now pushed into the post-sale phase.
 This shift means many models are essentially "semi-finished" at launch. Defects are no longer just traditional "build flaws" — they now include things that are "not yet finished."
 According to SAMR's Defective Product Administrative Center and public data, between March 2025 and March 2026, China saw 125 recall batches involving 3.5545 million vehicles — nearly 70% tied to software. Xiao Lingyun, head of the industrial products division at SAMR's Defective Product Recall Technical Center, explained at the 2026 China Auto Industry Development International Forum that as electrical and electronic architectures centralize and lines of code per vehicle grow exponentially, defect patterns have shifted from "linear wear" to "systemic collapse."
 Image source: Generated by Doubao
 Platform sharing further amplifies this "systemic collapse." Platformization is the core strategy for Chinese automakers to cut costs and boost efficiency, reusing a single architecture, supplier, and technical roadmap across multiple models to amortize R&D and procurement expenses.
 This model creates economies of scale in production, but it also introduces batch-level risks: having millions of vehicles across multiple models share the same design means a single defect can instantly hit millions of cars.
 These shifts in recalls aren't happening in a vacuum. To understand them, one must look at the increasingly compressed timeline behind these defects.
 From January to September 2026, China's auto industry generated revenue of 8.04 trillion yuan, up 2.6% year-on-year, while profits fell 23% to 267.5 billion yuan. The profit margin stood at 3.3%, below the 5.68% average for industrial enterprises of scale. In September alone, profits dropped 68% to 14.2 billion yuan, with a margin of 1.4% — a four-year low.
 With margins this thin, time has become the most direct competitive weapon. A three-month delay can mean missing a pricing window, so R&D cycles are being squeezed relentlessly. In the ICE era, cycles typically ran 36 to 60 months; now they've been compressed to 24, with some brands pushing 12 to 18. A full vehicle validation cycle, however, requires at least a year just for environmental adaptability — enduring "two winters and one summer" — plus full-scenario durability road testing, usually taking 12 to 18 months. As development timelines shrink, validation cycles are being compressed even further, with much physical testing replaced by simulation.
 Image source: Huaban
 For instance, during door handle testing at one automaker, only 2,000 of 10,000 tests were physical; the remaining 8,000 were simulated. Simulations can calculate stress distribution, but they can't replace time. What is lost in compression isn't necessarily recovered by computation.
 Yet it's worth noting that a shorter development cycle doesn't inherently mean lower quality.
 Lu Fang of VOYAH once stated that "short development time doesn't equal a rush-job car," a claim backed by evidence. Platformization, simulation, and domestic testing facilities do allow Chinese automakers to develop vehicles faster — and this has been one of the core competitive advantages of China's NEV sector in recent years.
 The real issue is the lack of a calibration mechanism between speed and validation — one that cannot be restored through corporate self-discipline alone.
 Who Pays the Price for Speed? 
 Without a self-correcting mechanism, the costs inevitably fall on specific links in the chain. The first to bear the brunt are the owners.
 Owners pay full price, yet the vehicle delivered may not be a finished product. Some software features are pushed later, and some edge cases only emerge during real-world use — risks that have already been transferred to the buyer at delivery. When Li Fenggang said "consumers have been turned into test drivers," this is exactly what he meant.
 Image source: Generated by Doubao
 Delivering "semi-finished" products and constantly patching them in pursuit of speed doesn't just degrade the immediate ownership experience — it also undermines the vehicle's long-term value.
 The most direct reflection is residual value. With rapid model iterations and frequent price adjustments, a car's used value can drop significantly after just three years. This loss never appears in a recall notice, but the owner absorbs it. Analyzing industry trends, Li Yanwei noted that the next phase of competition for Chinese automakers will hinge on systemic capabilities — after-sales, finance, parts supply, used-car residuals, and local production. The "rush-job" model is precisely overdrawing these long-term capabilities.
 Automakers are also paying for "speed," though the bill comes due later. Recalls have always been expensive. Take the 4.27 million-vehicle mega-recall: even at a cost of mere tens of yuan per vehicle, parts, labor, and logistics push the total past 100 million yuan, directly hitting quarterly earnings. But there's a fatal mismatch in the corporate ledger: costs saved during validation translate into immediate profit, while the real money lost to recalls falls on future periods. Relying on corporate self-discipline to fix this is clearly insufficient.
 Beyond that, the entire Chinese auto industry is paying a deeper, systemic price for this unhealthy pursuit of speed.
 First, when speed becomes the sole metric, automakers committed to long-termism and thorough validation lose out for being "too slow." This "bad money drives out good" dynamic is forcing the entire industry into a race on speed rather than quality. Second, if Chinese automakers carry these "rush-job" risks overseas, they risk heavy penalties under stringent regulations in mature markets, ultimately damaging the reputation of the "Chinese car" category. Finally, it forces tighter regulatory access. With regulators proactively uncovering over half of defects, it signals that internal industry screening mechanisms have partially failed. The resulting tightening of regulatory scrutiny translates into stricter market access thresholds for the entire sector.
 Conclusion: 
 How will the bill ultimately be settled? In the short term, costs appear to have been deftly distributed: automakers protect current profits, owners absorb residual losses and beta-testing risks, and the industry swallows internal friction and regulatory friction.
 But time borrowed against the laws of industrial manufacturing will eventually be repaid with interest. The months saved in validation could return as more frequent recalls, stricter access thresholds, and more fragile public trust. The four government bodies shifting the access logic from "meeting national standards is enough" to "full R&D validation is required for access" is a clear signal to bring these costs back to where they belong.
 Returning to the recall scam that opened this piece: the absurd fraud is certainly worth vigilance, but the deeper question for the industry is this — if the actual products were reliable enough, how could the word "recall" be so easily weaponized into a clickbait tool for panic and exploitation? A scam can be debunked with a single statement, but the trust fractured by product flaws takes a long time to mend.
